content: 1. A flow diagram is used to evaluate the feasibility of aggregating data at the national level. 2. If all clinics in the country are included in Early Warning Indicator (EWI) monitoring, the aggregated EWIs will be nationally representative. In this scenario, data can be readily aggregated across clinics. 3. If a subset of clinics is included through random sampling, the aggregated EWIs will still be nationally representative. However, data aggregation across clinics will require weighting to account for differences in clinic sizes. 4. If a subset of clinics is included through a combination of random sampling and convenience sampling, the aggregated EWIs will remain nationally representative. Data from randomly sampled clinics can be combined with data from conveniently sampled clinics using appropriate weighting methods. 5. If only conveniently sampled clinics are included, the aggregated EWIs will not be nationally representative. Data may be biased if the excluded clinics differ significantly from the included clinics. Aggregated EWIs should only be reported if data availability exceeds the recommended 70% threshold. 6. If only conveniently sampled clinics are included, the data may still be considered nationally representative if the conveniently sampled clinics represent more than 70% of the eligible patient population for each indicator. 7. For clinics using paper-based medical records, clinic staff trained in the national EWI monitoring strategy should abstract data at their respective sites. Data abstraction is typically performed retrospectively, once per year. 8. Whenever possible, countries should integrate EWI data abstraction with other indicator and patient monitoring activities already occurring in the country. 9. EWI monitoring can also serve as, or be combined with, a quality assurance assessment of record-keeping practices at ART clinics. 10. For clinics using electronic medical records (EMRs), experts from the national program should guide the data abstraction process for EWI monitoring. 11. It is generally not feasible to obtain EWI information directly from summary reports produced by electronic record-keeping systems due to variations in indicator definitions and methods of applying these definitions. 12. If EMRs are used to produce EWIs, validation procedures involving abstraction from paper records should be established. 13. When electronic query programs are developed, they must track available data and classify clinics with more than 30% missing data for a particular indicator as grey. 14. Electronic query programs must also monitor the overall proportion of missing data across all clinics to assess the feasibility of national aggregation for a specific EWI. 15. Data quality should be assessed throughout the EWI monitoring process. 16. During data abstraction, data quality assessments are critical to ensure that the correct data are abstracted appropriately. 17. After data analysis and reporting, data quality assessments provide program and clinic managers with confidence in the results and determine the fitness of the data for operational use, planning, and decision-making. 18. Data reliability assesses the dependability of data abstracted for each indicator. Identifying quality issues early in the monitoring process allows for corrective actions, such as additional support or training. 19. Data completeness refers to the extent of missing information in patient records. While some missing data are expected, a high percentage of missing information for any EWI at a clinic poses challenges for achieving the required sample size and interpreting results. 20. Monitoring data completeness during the abstraction process is essential. Clinics with less than 70% available data for any indicator should report a grey score for that indicator. 21. A grey score is not punitive but indicates that the clinic requires support in record-keeping to fully benefit from indicator monitoring. Aggregation should not be performed unless at least 70% of data are available from all sampled sites. 22. Data consistency refers to the uniformity of patient information across different record systems within the same clinic. 23. Clinic and pharmacy records are the primary sources of information for EWI monitoring. Some clinics use both paper-based and electronic systems for these records. 24. A records assessment process should be conducted before data abstraction to evaluate the consistency of information across these sources. This step is crucial for identifying the most accurate sources of information. 25. Data quality assessments, while not specifically designed for EWI monitoring, identify strengths and weaknesses in existing record systems at participating clinics. 26. Incomplete or inconsistent data often indicate systemic problems in record-keeping that need to be addressed. 27. The results of data quality assessments can inform changes to improve patient monitoring systems and clinic practices.
